item.title: The 1930 Tariff Law Nobody Had Used — Until Canadian Hockey Sticks Made the List
item.body:
For most of the last century, Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 was the kind of provision trade lawyers mentioned at conferences and then moved on from. It is on the books. It has real teeth. And in roughly 96 years, no president had ever used it to actually put a duty on anything.

That changes on **August 19**, when a **50% duty** invoked under Section 338 is scheduled to take effect on a specific list of Canadian goods: passenger vehicles, dairy products, wine, cement — and hockey sticks.

The product list is what gets the headlines. The legal mechanism is what matters.

---

## What Section 338 actually says

Section 338 is codified at 19 U.S.C. § 1338, part of the same 1930 statute better known by the names of its sponsors, Smoot and Hawley. Its subject is not national security, not trade deficits, and not unfair subsidies. It is *discrimination*.

In plain terms, the provision allows the president to respond when a foreign country is found to impose burdens or restrictions on US commerce that place American exporters at a disadvantage relative to other countries. The available responses are unusually blunt for US trade law:

- **New or additional duties of up to 50% ad valorem** on that country's products, and
- in the more extreme case, **exclusion of the goods from entry altogether**.

The statute also contemplates a fact-finding role for the US International Trade Commission in identifying such discriminatory practices and reporting them. But compared with the tools Washington has leaned on for the past decade, the procedural runway is short.

That contrast is the reason this is a story at all. **Section 232** requires a Commerce Department national-security investigation. **Section 301** requires a formal USTR proceeding, notice, comment, and a hearing. Emergency economic powers require a declared emergency — and have drawn sustained litigation over whether the tariff power was ever in that statute to begin with. Section 338 sits outside all of those frameworks, with its own findings requirement and its own ceiling.

For years, the standard explanation for why nobody used it was that it wasn't needed. The modern toolkit was broader, better-tested in court, and easier to defend. The revival of a 1930 authority suggests the calculation has shifted toward statutes that haven't been narrowed by decades of case law — precisely because they haven't been tested.

---

## Why this round is different: the USMCA carve-out is gone

Every significant US tariff action against Canada in recent years came with the same escape hatch. If a shipment qualified as originating under the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement — if it met the rules of origin and the exporter or importer could certify it — the goods came in outside the new duty.

That carve-out did enormous work. It is why a Canadian-assembled vehicle with a qualifying regional value content was treated differently from an identical-looking vehicle sourced elsewhere. It is why compliance departments across the continent spent 2025 and early 2026 rebuilding bills of materials rather than rerouting supply chains.

**The Section 338 action, as announced, contains no such exemption.** A good that satisfies every USMCA rule of origin — a car meeting the regional value content and labor value content thresholds, a cheese produced entirely in Quebec, a stick laid up in an Ontario plant — is covered on the same terms as a good that doesn't.

That is the substantive change. Not the rate. The rate is high, but rates move. What moved here is the *status* of a document.

---

## The certificate of origin stops being a shield

Since NAFTA took effect in 1994, and continuing under USMCA from July 2020, North American trade has run on a shared assumption: prove where a good comes from, and the tariff schedule follows automatically. USMCA even simplified the mechanics, replacing NAFTA's standardized form with a certification of origin that an importer, exporter, or producer can issue based on a set of required data elements.

That certification became the load-bearing beam of continental manufacturing. Auto programs were sourced around it. Food processors structured contracts around it. Customs brokers built practices around it.

A duty that applies regardless of origin certification doesn't repeal any of that. But it does demote it. The paperwork still governs preferential *duty-free* treatment under the agreement. It no longer guarantees that a shipment escapes whatever else has been layered on top.

If you want one sentence for why trade counsel are re-reading old statutes this month, it is this: **origin compliance has stopped being a complete answer to the question "what will this cost at the border?"**

---

## The joint-review backdrop

None of this is happening in a vacuum. USMCA was written with a clock in it.

The agreement entered into force on July 1, 2020, with a 16-year term and a **joint review at the six-year mark** — July 1, 2026. If all three parties confirm they want to extend, the term rolls forward another 16 years. If they don't, the agreement doesn't collapse; it shifts into a cycle of **annual reviews** running toward a 2036 endpoint, with the parties expected to keep trying to resolve their differences in the meantime.

Washington's decision not to renew the pact in its current form puts the agreement into exactly that annual-review posture. The treaty is still in force. Its obligations still exist. But its long horizon — the thing that made it worth designing a 10-year vehicle program around — is now provisional, reviewed one year at a time.

Layer the Section 338 duty on top of that, and the message businesses are reading is less about a single 50% number and more about **planning horizon**. A tariff can be reversed next quarter. A twelve-month review cycle is a structural feature.

---

## Who feels it, and how unevenly

The five categories on the list are not equivalent, and the volumes tell you something about intent.

**Vehicles** are the heavyweight. Canadian assembly plants ship a large share of their output south, and the integrated parts networks around Ontario and Michigan mean components can cross the border several times before a finished car does. A duty applied without an origin exemption interacts badly with a supply chain that was deliberately built to be continental.

**Dairy** is the outlier by volume. The United States generally runs a *surplus* in dairy trade with Canada — US processors sell more north than Canadian processors sell south. A tariff on Canadian dairy therefore isn't primarily about the flow it taxes. It reads as pressure on a long-running dispute over how Canada allocates its tariff-rate quotas under its supply-management system, an issue that has already been through formal dispute settlement.

**Wine** is small in dollar terms — Niagara and Okanagan producers ship modest volumes — but highly visible on retail shelves, and it sits inside a broader argument about provincial liquor-board practices that US exporters have complained about for years.

**Cement** is the quiet one with the largest downstream footprint. Canada is among the biggest sources of imported cement in the US, and it moves into Great Lakes, Northeast, and Pacific Northwest markets where the freight economics of alternative suppliers are poor. Construction input costs don't make headlines the way car prices do, but they reach further.

**Hockey sticks** are the item everyone will remember, and the one with the most instructive complication. Several of the best-known brands are Canadian in identity and headquarters, while a great deal of composite stick manufacturing happens in Asia. Whether a given stick is "Canadian" for customs purposes depends on where it was actually made and how the origin rules treat it — which is to say, the symbolic item on the list is also a small lesson in why origin analysis is harder than a logo.

---

## What is still genuinely unsettled

A few things are worth holding loosely until they're confirmed in the operative documents:

- **Stacking.** Whether the 50% applies on top of existing sector duties, or in place of them, changes the landed cost dramatically. Check the proclamation text and the customs guidance, not summaries.
- **Scope by tariff line.** "Cars" and "dairy" are categories in a press summary; what binds is the list of HTS subheadings. Adjacent products often turn out to be in or out in ways the category label doesn't predict.
- **In-transit treatment.** Actions like this usually specify how goods already on the water or on a rail car are handled. That detail decides who eats the cost on shipments already booked.
- **Legal challenge.** A statute unused for 96 years has correspondingly little case law defining its limits — the findings required, how specific they must be, and how far judicial review reaches. Litigation is a reasonable expectation, and its outcome is not predictable from the text alone.
- **Response.** Canada has its own retaliation authorities and a domestic political timetable of its own. The list above may not be the last list.

---

## What to watch over the next two weeks

Between now and August 19, the useful signals are administrative rather than rhetorical: the published proclamation and its annexes, US Customs and Border Protection guidance messages to the trade community, any exclusion or drawback process, and the tariff-line detail. Statements from either capital will move sentiment; the annexes will move invoices.

The longer-term signal is the annual review cycle. A single duty on five product categories is a discrete event. A framework in which the continent's trade rulebook is reconfirmed twelve months at a time is a different operating environment — and it is the part that will still be true after this particular tariff is resolved, whichever way it goes.

The hockey sticks will get the jokes. The certificate of origin is the story.

---

*This article is general information about a public policy development, not legal, tax, customs, or investment advice. Tariff actions change quickly and the operative details are set by the published proclamation and official customs guidance. Importers and exporters should confirm current requirements with the Federal Register, US Customs and Border Protection, and qualified trade counsel before making decisions.*
